html:
Leiden University, the oldest university in the Netherlands, was founded in 1575 by William the Silent. By tradition it was a reward to the city for holding out against a Spanish siege the year before.

In the Golden Age Leiden drew students and scholars from across Protestant Europe, helped by the freedom of the Dutch printing trade. Hugo Grotius studied there as a boy, and Descartes lived nearby. Its botanical garden and its anatomy theatre were famous, and Herman Boerhaave made its medical school the leading one of Europe in the early 1700s.

Its scholars of Arabic and Asian languages helped found European oriental studies. In 1940 the law professor Rudolph Cleveringa protested against the dismissal of Jewish colleagues under the German occupation, and the university was closed. See the Netherlands.
